structure.title: 5. Job loss and DV (descriptives, identification, dynamic effects, under-reporting, robustness, heterogeneity, couples)
6. Unemployment benefits and DV (RD design, balance, results and robustness)

observations.statement: Two designs are announced up front: a difference-in-differences around mass layoffs (with matched never-treated controls) for job loss, and a regression discontinuity at an eligibility cutoff for unemployment benefits; the RD coefficient is explicitly labelled an intention-to-treat effect of eligibility.

The main threat to the DiD is named as dynamic selection into displacement; the authors state that parallel pre-trends attenuate but do not fully address it and argue that mass layoffs depend on firm-level shocks rather than individual behaviour.

The stacked design centred on treatment timing with never-treated controls is presented as the answer to staggered two-way fixed effects concerns, citing the recent methodological literature, with alternative estimators promised in the appendix.

For the RD, the authors explain why a different eligibility cutoff cannot be used (documented manipulation elsewhere) and why the running-variable density shows periodic discontinuities due to monthly dismissal cycles, motivating the baseline sample restriction on initial dismissal dates.

Endogenous reporting of DV is presented as the first-order concern and is signposted in the introduction, with the direction of bias for male and female job loss spelled out before the evidence is shown.

Court registers (from a private information provider compiling public tribunal data) are linked to the universe of formal employment records over a stated period by full name; the paper explains that names are consistently recorded in both registers.

The linkage sample is restricted to individuals with a nationally unique name; uniqueness is measured by combining employment and welfare registers, and selection into this subsample is assessed with standardized differences against non-unique-name job losers (appendix table).

Jurisdictions with a very high share of missing defendant or victim names are dropped in the main analysis; the paper explains the two sources of missingness (data entry and judicial secrecy) and argues in a footnote why secrecy is unlikely to relate to job status.

The DiD uses a perfectly balanced worker-year panel from several years before to several years after layoff, with treated workers displaced in mass layoffs in the central years of the sample period; controls are exact-matched on cohort, tenure, earnings bin, firm size quartile, sector and state, with one random control drawn when several match.

The RD sample widens name uniqueness to the state level to gain power, stops before a year of major UI reforms, keeps workers who exhausted prior benefits (to strengthen the first stage), and restricts initial dismissal dates to mid-month days to avoid dismissal cycles overlapping the cutoff.
Observation counts are reported in every panel of the main tables and in the descriptive table.
Firms that reappear under a new identifier are excluded from the mass-layoff definition using a stated reallocation rule, and the definition is tied to prior displacement literature.

Mass layoff is defined by a firm-size floor and a minimum share of the workforce dismissed without just cause in a year; the layoff date is shifted earlier by the statutory notice period, described as a conservative choice for pre-trend testing.

DV outcomes are yearly indicators of appearing as defendant in a DV suit (men) or as victim in a protective measure (women); relative-time dummies are built from exact layoff and case dates rather than calendar years.

The RD running variable is time elapsed since the previous UI-generating layoff, centred at the eligibility threshold; treatment is an eligibility indicator, and the polynomial is allowed to differ on each side of the cutoff.

Three alternative DV measures are constructed to limit reporting discretion: in flagrante cases, public shelter use from the welfare registry, and mandatory health-system notifications; the last is linked without individual identifiers via clusters of birth date, municipality and gender, with validation in the appendix.

tags: other:severance pay imputed from tenure and earnings
observations.statement: Severance pay is not observed directly; it is imputed from tenure and earnings using the statutory formula and used to motivate tenure-group heterogeneity.

The main DiD table reports the coefficient, the treated-group mean at the reference period, the effect relative to that mean, an elasticity to earnings and N per column; the notes list the included regressors (treatment dummy, year fixed effects) and the firm-level clustering.

The RD table is organized in panels (first stage on UI payments, DV after layoff, DV before layoff as placebo, employment), each reporting the mean at the cutoff, the relative effect and N; notes describe the bandwidth, the local linear terms and individual-level clustering.
A footnote notes that adding individual fixed effects or calendar-time fixed effects leaves the DiD coefficients unchanged, which is used to justify the sparse baseline specification.

tags: other:all estimates rescaled by treated baseline mean
observations.statement: All estimates throughout the paper are rescaled by the treated-group outcome mean in the year before layoff; a footnote motivates this relative-effects convention by under-reporting of DV and by parallel practice in the crime literature.

DiD standard errors are clustered at the firm level and RD standard errors at the individual level, stated only in table notes; no explicit justification for either cluster level is given in the text.
For the RD, permutation tests compare the estimate at the true cutoff with a distribution of estimates at placebo cutoffs, announced in the design section and reported in an appendix figure.
When comparing male and female job loss effects, the paper re-estimates both on a common smaller sample and reports a test of equality, noting that the female sample is smaller and less precise.

A main-text table compares treated and matched controls on demographics, job and area characteristics and pre-period DV using standardized differences with a stated threshold from Imbens and Rubin, and also compares mass-layoff workers with all displaced workers for external validity.

Event-study figures with anticipation coefficients for several pre-periods are the main pre-trend evidence; additional pre-trend tests and quarterly-frequency estimates are placed in the appendix, and the authors note that third-party DV measures allow cleaner pre-trend inspection than court suits.
observations.locator: Figures 2, 3, 5; Section 5.5 fn. 44; Supplementary Appendix C.6.I, C.6.J

observations.statement: RD validity is supported by a density plot with the McCrary test and the bias-robust local polynomial density test, plus covariate balance at the cutoff, all in appendix figures; the pre-displacement DV placebo panel is in the main table.
observations.locator: Section 6.2; Supplementary Figures D1, D2; Table 3 Panel C

observations.statement: The RD first stage (UI payments by semester, total payments, take-up) is reported as Panel A of the main RD table and in the top row of the RD figure before the outcome results.
Pre-layoff DV outcomes are used as a placebo panel within the main RD table, mirroring the structure of the post-layoff panel semester by semester.

Sensitivity to bandwidths and polynomial orders (including the CCT optimal bandwidth), placebo cutoffs, and a specification with cutoff-date and dismissal-date fixed effects are all reported in appendix tables and figures and summarized in one sentence in the text.
observations.locator: Section 6.3; Supplementary Tables D1, D2; Figure D3

observations.statement: Robustness is a numbered list in a dedicated subsection (ten items) pointing to appendix subsections: matching on education and reweighting, municipality-industry-year fixed effects, stricter layoff definitions and plant closures, an ITT at the firm level, spillover checks, missing names, name uniqueness, staggered DiD estimators, rare-outcome estimators, pre-trend tests.
observations.locator: Section 5.5; Supplementary Appendix C.6.A to C.6.J

observations.statement: The robustness discussion candidly states that point estimates vary to some extent across checks but keep the same sign and order of magnitude, rather than claiming exact stability.
observations.quote: point estimates vary to some extent with these tests

observations.statement: For the RD, the authors distinguish which result is robust (the second-semester effect) from which is less robust (the cumulative three-year effect), stating this explicitly in the text.
To compare the RD and DiD populations, the RD sample is reweighted by entropy balancing to match the job-loss sample and the DV results re-estimated in an appendix table.
observations.locator: Section 6.3 fn. 57; Supplementary Tables D3, D4

observations.statement: Heterogeneity by age, education, income and tenure is shown for men only (female subgroups judged too imprecise); a second specification interacts all DiD coefficients with third-order polynomials in the other characteristics to separate correlated dimensions, and area-level heterogeneity is in the appendix.
observations.locator: Section 5.6 fn. 45; Figure 6; Supplementary Figures C12 to C14

observations.statement: The tenure gradient is used as a test of the income mechanism because severance rises with tenure; the authors check that the employment effect does not vary across the same groups to rule out an exposure explanation.

A two-period model with two named mechanisms yields propositions that are mapped to specific empirical tests (tenure gradient, dynamic UI effects by semester); a separate discussion section then confronts results with competing DV theories and argues each single mechanism alone cannot fit all patterns.
Survey data are used in the appendix to document time spent together by partners when one is unemployed and to gauge informal-sector income recovery, supporting model assumptions.

Couples-level analyses check partner employment (added worker effect) and separation; a related exercise on cohabitation after a DV filing is explicitly labelled non-causal because treatment is endogenous.

Effects are expressed relative to the treated baseline mean and as elasticities to earnings; the introduction benchmarks the size against cash-transfer and divorce-law studies in a footnote, and the UI benefit is expressed in months of payments and pre-displacement wages.

Precision is discussed directly: female estimates are described as less precise, subgroup coefficients as not significantly different from one another, and the focus on men in the RD is justified by imprecision for women rather than by a null.

Acknowledged limits include no administrative data on informal work, missing names in court data, restriction to unique names, and lack of individual identifiers in health notifications; each is paired with a mitigation exercise.
The absence of a separation effect is qualified by a possible lack of statistical power given the small share of women affected, and results based on endogenous DV timing are flagged as non-causal.

External validity of mass-layoff estimates is addressed by comparing them with all displaced workers in the balance table, by state-level name samples and reweighting, and the RD sample is compared and reweighted to the DiD sample.

Figures are event-study plots with confidence bands, binned RD plots with local linear fits, and coefficient plots by subgroup; tables use significance stars and notes restate the sample, comparison group, regressors and clustering; figure notes repeat the treatment and control definitions each time.

A descriptive section opens the results with raw plots of DV by employment status, age and tenure, explicitly warning that raw differences mix causal effects and selection; the descriptive table doubles as the balance table.
Supplementary material is referenced by lettered appendix sections and numbered tables and figures (B, C, D prefixes); the supplement is not part of the article PDF.

The introduction previews the main results, mechanisms and the model, summarizes how identification threats are addressed, contains a labelled related-literature subsection with a distinct contribution paragraph, and ends with a roadmap.

Order is model, context, data, then for each design: identification, main dynamic results, measurement checks, robustness subsection, heterogeneity; a mechanisms discussion follows both designs; most robustness detail lives in the supplement.

tags: other:each result tied to a model proposition
observations.statement: Each empirical section states which model proposition it tests, and the mechanisms section revisits results proposition by proposition.
A data availability statement says most data are restricted Brazilian records; a Zenodo package with code, instructions for obtaining restricted data, and the shareable data portion is cited by DOI.
Stata packages used for the analysis (gtools, reghdfe/ftools, rdrobust, did_multiplegt, ebalance, estout) are cited in a footnote and listed in the references.

Data are administrative registers (employment, UI payments, welfare registry, health notifications) plus court records purchased from a private provider; all are cited as dataset references with years in the bibliography.
Ethics approval from a university review board is reported with a protocol number in the acknowledgments.
One piece of supporting evidence (dismissal-cycle density patterns) is described as available upon request rather than included in the supplement.
